reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Presents with massive colonic distension, abdominal pain and often reduced bowel sounds in the absence of a mechanical obstructing lesion
Typically occurs in hospitalised or postoperative patients and those with serious systemic illness, trauma or electrolyte disturbance
Imaging shows marked dilatation of the caecum and right colon, and the risk of ischaemia and perforation rises sharply as caecal diameter increases
A mechanical obstruction and toxic megacolon must be excluded before making the diagnosis, often with water-soluble contrast or CT
Initial management is supportive with correction of electrolytes, review of opioids and other contributing drugs, and bowel rest with decompression
Neostigmine or decompression for Ogilvie is used when conservative measures fail and there is no perforation or ischaemia, with colonoscopic decompression as an alternative
Serial abdominal examination and imaging are essential to detect impending caecal perforation early
reference.pathophysiology: Ogilvie syndrome is a massive dilatation of the colon without a mechanical cause, arising from an imbalance in autonomic innervation of the colon. Excess sympathetic tone and reduced parasympathetic (sacral) drive impair colonic motility, particularly in the distal colon, producing a functional obstruction and gross proximal dilatation that is most pronounced in the caecum and right colon. It is precipitated by severe illness, surgery, trauma, metabolic and electrolyte disturbances and drugs that impair motility such as opioids. As the caecum has the largest diameter and thinnest wall, rising wall tension there threatens ischaemia and perforation.
additionalDifferentials: Mechanical colonic obstruction from tumour, stricture or volvulus
Paralytic ileus involving the small bowel
additionalInvestigations: Abdominal radiograph to assess colonic and caecal diameter
CT abdomen or water-soluble contrast enema to exclude mechanical obstruction
Electrolytes including potassium, magnesium, calcium and phosphate
Thyroid function and review of the drug chart for opioids and anticholinergics
Serial examination and imaging to monitor caecal diameter
redFlags: Progressive caecal dilatation approaching diameters associated with perforation
Peritonism, fever or rising inflammatory markers suggesting ischaemia or perforation
Marked tenderness localised to the right iliac fossa over the caecum
reference.prognosis: With prompt recognition and treatment most cases resolve without surgery, but delayed diagnosis complicated by caecal ischaemia or perforation carries a high mortality.
pitfalls: Assuming mechanical obstruction and failing to consider a functional cause, or vice versa
Giving neostigmine when perforation or ischaemia is present or unexcluded
Neglecting to correct electrolyte disturbances and reduce opioids
Underestimating caecal diameter and missing impending perforation
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy guidance on acute colonic pseudo-obstruction
management: Supportive first-line care with bowel rest, nil by mouth and nasogastric plus rectal-tube decompression
Correct precipitating electrolyte disturbances (potassium, magnesium, calcium, phosphate) and treat the underlying illness or sepsis
Review and minimise contributing drugs, especially opioids and anticholinergics, and mobilise the patient
Exclude mechanical obstruction, toxic megacolon, ischaemia and perforation with water-soluble contrast enema or CT before pharmacological treatment
Pharmacological decompression with intravenous neostigmine when conservative measures fail, under cardiac monitoring with atropine available for bradycardia
Colonoscopic decompression for refractory cases or marked caecal dilatation
Serial examination and imaging to track caecal diameter, escalating to surgery (caecostomy or colectomy) for ischaemia or perforation
